subject: Bayesian spatial modeling with INLA using two likelihoods of data with unequal sample size

messages.author: cdaedda7d73defe4
messages.subject: Bayesian spatial modeling with INLA using two likelihoods of data with unequal sample size
parts:
Hi Professor Rue and Dear INLA users,

I have some questions about the Bayesian modeling based on INLA using multiple likelihoods.

When reading the following two papers:

- Martins TG, Simpson D, Lindgren F, Rue H (2013) Bayesian computing with INLA: New features. Computational Statistics & Data Analysis 67:68–83. doi: 10.1016/j.csda.2013.04.014

- Illian JB, Martino S, Sørbye SH, et al (2013) Fitting complex ecological point process models with integrated nested Laplace approximation. Methods in Ecology and Evolution 4:305–315. doi: 10.1111/2041-21...@10.1111/(ISSN)2041-210X.STATSTOO,

I found out that it is possible to fit Bayesian models with INLA using multiple likelihoods. For all the cas studies above, the sample size of the data giving the two likelihoods are equal.
A typical example in forestry is the marked point process models (see Illian et al. 2013), where in addition to the observed individuals (i.e. spatial locations of a species, which is modelled by point process likelihood), we have additional information related to the health status of each species (modeled by binomial likelihood) or the diameter of each species (which can be modeled by Gaussian likelihood).

However, let's suppose that, the data available for the second likelihood is aggregated in grid cells (e.g. a regular lattice), such that its sample size (say m) is less than the one of the first data (say n), of which individuals are observed at each spatial location. As example, see the Dorazio's approach proposed in Species Distribution Models [Dorazio RM (2014) Accounting for imperfect detection and survey bias in statistical analysis of presence‐only data. Global Ecology and Biogeography 23:1472–1484. doi: 10.1111/geb.12216], which includes two likelihoods: Poisson point process likelihood for the presence-only data observed at each location and Poisson likelihood for the point-counts from planned survey (i.e. aggregated data in each lattice/grid cell). The idea was to jointly model the two datases.
Ne
My questions are as follows:

- Is it possible to apply the Dorazio approach with INLA using the multiple likelihoods framework of Martins et al. (2013)? And how to do it (any attempt of R code) ?

- Can the INLA handle the sampling bias (using thinned point process models) along with imperfect detection issue as proposed in Dorazio (2014) or do we need INLABRU for that ?

Any answers or clarifications will be very appreciated.


Best.

--

messages.author: 3eab71733027a24a
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Bayesian spatial modeling with INLA using two likelihoods of data with unequal sample size
parts:
Hi,

I don't know the details of the Dorazio approach, as soon you're
thinking of a thinned point process, where you also have to estimate
some parameters in the 'how to thin', then INLABRU was essentially
written to target this question, as an extention of the original INLA
algorithm. (and it does other things as well, of'course)

messages.author: cdaedda7d73defe4
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Bayesian spatial modeling with INLA using two likelihoods of data with unequal sample size
parts:
Hi,

Thank for your reply.

In fact, Dorazio approach is a joint modeling in frequentist framework. The model involves two likelihoods: a poisson process likelihood for the occurrence of a given species observed at each spatial location and a poisson likelihood for the point-counts that are observed in some quadrats over the same study region. 

Here is the paper of Dorazio, in which all the math is developped:
Dorazio RM (2014) Accounting for imperfect detection and survey bias in statistical analysis of presence‐only data. Global Ecology and Biogeography 23:1472–1484. doi:10.1111/geb.12216
